newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kuehbacher wants close adherence to EMU criteria.
newsitem.headline: Kuehbacher wants close adherence to EMU criteria.

text.p: Bundesbank council member Klaus-Dieter Kuehbacher on Monday warned against an overly-generous interpretation of the criteria for membership of European Economic and Monetary Union.

"If investor confidence is undermined and price stability in international financial markets is brought into doubt, then we must expect high levels of turbulence on the markets before January 1 1999," Kuehbacher said in the text of a speech.

Kuehbacher, also head of the state central bank in Berlin and Brandenburg, went on to say that neither Germany or France would meet the government debt and deficit criteria in 1997 for membership of European currency union.

He was referring to Maastricht treaty criteria which require that European Union member nations aim for budget deficits of no more than three percent of gross domestic product and a government debt of no more than 60 percent of GDP in 1997 to join EMU at its launch.

The Maastricht treaty allowed room for an overshoot, in exceptional circumstances, on the entry requirement that EU member nations aim for budget deficits of no more than three percent of GDP in 1997 to join EMU at its launch, Kuehbacher said.
However, he said that the dangers of market turbulence could only be avoided if European governments and central banks insisted on a "clear and strict interpretation" of the Maastricht criteria.

Kuehbacher said that German state deficits of 3.8 percent in 1996 and 3.5 percent the previous year had led to the question of whether or not the criteria laid out in the Maastricht treaty should be given a "more generous reading."

He said that not only would a softening on EMU criteria lead to dire economic consequences, but provisions on the issue in the German constitution meant a close reading of the convergence criteria was legally required.
"A softening of convergence criteria cannot be considered an option, on both economic and constitutional grounds," Kuehbacher said.

Kuehbacher said that estimates for German tax revenues, due this month, would show Germany's budget deficit at between 3.2 percent and 3.5 percent of GDP and said that he expected this figure because of the high level of tax shortfalls and increased social welfare spending.
He said that it was possible that the German government would raise taxes to help German meet the criteria.
